results.claim: Almost all reinforcement learning methods are well described as generalized policy iteration (GPI).

limits: Classical DP assumes a perfect model and is computationally expensive, so of limited utility in RL itself but a theoretical foundation (p.73).
Whether policy iteration or value iteration is better in general is not clear (p.87).
Gridworld and gambler results are illustrations; no timing or iteration counts are given beyond the figures; gambler threshold theta not stated.
Exact solutions for continuous state/action spaces are possible only in special cases; quantization is the common approach (p.73).
Figures: million-state capacity claim reflects 2018 hardware.
practices: Use the in-place (Gauss-Seidel) version of iterative policy evaluation; it usually converges faster than two arrays (Sec 4.1).
Stop iterative policy evaluation when max|v_{k+1}-v_k| < theta (Sec 4.1 pseudocode).
Start each policy evaluation in policy iteration from the previous policy's value function (Sec 4.3).
Truncate policy evaluation, as in value iteration with one sweep, without losing convergence (Sec 4.4).
Interpose several evaluation sweeps between improvement sweeps for faster convergence (Sec 4.4).
Prefer asynchronous DP on large state spaces, focusing updates on states the agent visits (Sec 4.5, 4.7).
Policy iteration pseudocode can cycle among equally good policies; fix the termination for real use (Exercise 4.4).

code.snippet: Iterative Policy Evaluation: Loop: Delta<-0; for each s: v<-V(s); V(s)<-sum_a pi(a|s) sum_{s',r} p(s',r|s,a)[r+gamma V(s')]; Delta<-max(Delta,|v-V(s)|) until Delta<theta

Policy Iteration: 1 Initialization; 2 Policy Evaluation (loop until Delta<theta); 3 Policy Improvement: pi(s)<-argmax_a sum p(s',r|s,a)[r+gamma V(s')]; if policy-stable return V~v*, pi~pi*, else go to 2
v_{k+1}(s) = max_a sum_{s',r} p(s',r|s,a)[r + gamma v_k(s')]; output pi(s)=argmax_a sum p(s',r|s,a)[r+gamma V(s')]
